contributions.text_english: 1. What steps is the Welsh Government taking to support the expansion of library services in Clwyd? OQ64690
contributions.text_original: 1. Pa gamau mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i gefnogi'r gwaith o ehangu gwasanaethau llyfrgell yng Nghlwyd? OQ64690

contributions.text_english: Local authorities have a statutory responsibility to provide a comprehensive and efficient library service. The Welsh Government supports libraries in Clwyd through capital and revenue funding. In 2026-27, this includes awarding £349,000 to fund capital improvements in Colwyn Bay library and Rhyl library. Libraries across Clwyd have also benefited this year from over £50,000 of funding for smaller projects.
contributions.text_original: Mae gan awdurdodau lleol gyfrifoldeb statudol i ddarparu gwasanaeth llyfrgell cynhwysfawr ac effeithlon. Mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn cefnogi llyfrgelloedd yng Nghlwyd drwy gyllid cyfalaf a refeniw. Yn 2026-27, mae hyn yn cynnwys dyfarnu £349,000 i ariannu gwelliannau cyfalaf yn llyfrgell Bae Colwyn a llyfrgell y Rhyl. Mae llyfrgelloedd ledled Clwyd hefyd wedi elwa eleni o dros £50,000 o gyllid ar gyfer prosiectau llai.

contributions.text_english: Thank you, Minister. A local authority in Clwyd in 2023 resolved to reduce library one-stop shop opening hours by 40 per cent. This was despite over 4,500 residents responding to the consultation—the most that the local authority had seen in years. Ninety per cent of those responses warned that the closure or reduction in hours would limit their ability to visit their local library, and 96 per cent of these submissions submitted negative comments about the proposal. The local authority went ahead because its hands, to a certain extent, were tied financially by the funding formula. The significant change has seen around £360,000 saved but severely limits residents' access to this important service. So, what steps are you taking to support local library services, and what discussions have you had with the Minister for local government on seeing a funding formula that specifically protects library services? Diolch.

The Member raises an important issue, I know, for many of our constituents across Wales. I do acknowledge the challenges that local authorities have faced because of the financial settlements of these past years and the impact that that has had on local libraries in particular. One of the things that we are doing as part of our work in developing the culture and sports strategy is looking at local services. I have had discussions already with some local government leaders in Wales and the Welsh Local Government Association, in order to try and truly understand how fragile some of these services are.

Central to our new strategy is ensuring equal access for everyone. So, we want to understand what these challenges have been over past years, what that has meant to services in terms of libraries across Wales. A large part of our next piece of work will involve looking at that long-term strategy in terms of what library services that work for our communities look like, recognising that the service doesn't always meet our ambition in all parts of Wales at the moment.

contributions.text_english: Libraries are essential services for young and old, often going far past the borrowing of books by providing warm spaces and tackling social isolation. The Public Libraries and Museums Act 1964 places a statutory duty on councils in England and Wales to provide a comprehensive and efficient library service. However, discussions with people in the sector suggest that a lack of clarity around what this actually means creates ambiguity and can lead to library provision being treated as discretionary rather than a legal duty. I think you have gone some way to answering the question in terms of that long-term strategy, but would the Government consider looking to give more clarity on what constitutes a comprehensive and efficient library service and provide councils with greater certainty about their statutory responsibilities?

As the work of developing the new strategy goes forward, we will also be publishing specific plans looking at every sector, including libraries, in order to provide more clarity, yes, to local authorities, but also to the people of Wales.

contributions.text_english: 2. How is the Welsh Government protecting and promoting national monuments in Gwynedd Maldwyn for future generations? OQ64676

contributions.text_english: Cadw protects and promotes nationally important monuments in Gwynedd Maldwyn through designation and through providing expert advice, guidance and support to the owners for their conservation. Cadw also promotes our heritage by managing the national monuments in its care and ensuring public access to them, in accordance with this Government's commitment to provide fair access to all of our cultural and heritage sites.

Mae Cadw hefyd yn hyrwyddo ein treftadaeth drwy reoli'r henebion cenedlaethol sydd yn ei ofal a sicrhau mynediad cyhoeddus atyn nhw, yn unol ag ymrwymiad y Llywodraeth hon i hyrwyddo mynediad teg i'n safleoedd diwylliannol a threftadaeth.

contributions.text_english: You will be aware that Llansilin in the Gwynedd Maldwyn constituency is the home of Sycharth, the ancient court of Owain Glyndŵr and one of the most significant sites of our national heritage. Unfortunately, however, it is disgraceful that the current state of the site doesn't reflect its historic and national importance. There are problems such as overgrowing foliage, lack of access and even a lack of mention of the site on the Cadw website. On the other hand, Powys council has already rejected proposals for more signage on the road to promote the site. Can I ask, therefore, how the Welsh Government can work with Cadw and Powys County Council to ensure that Sycharth is promoted as a site of national importance for future generations?

Ceir problemau megis gordyfiant, diffyg mynediad hygyrch, a hyd yn oed diffyg crybwyll i'r safle ar wefan Cadw. contributions.text_english: I thank the Member for raising the issue of Sycharth. Just to be clear, I do consider Sycharth to be a monument of national importance that has a very significant place in Wales's history and in our identity as a nation. The monument is open to the public. There are interpretation signs on the site. After a conservation programme carried out with funding by Cadw, work has gone ahead since concerns were raised a few years ago. However, I am on the record as saying that I would like to see more being done to promote Sycharth before I was in this role, and I'm still of that opinion. Even though the rural location and nature of the site do present some problems in terms of physical access and the way it's presented, I have asked Cadw to look into how we can make the story of this site more prominent, because it is just so important in terms of our history. You will also be aware that Sycharth isn't for sale at the moment. It has a lifetime tenancy. Cadw is working in partnership with the estate that owns Sycharth to ensure that it is maintained and kept in good condition and that public access continues.

Mae yna arwyddion dehongli ar y safle. Yn sgil rhaglen o waith cadwraeth a gynhaliwyd gyda chyllid gan Cadw, mae yna waith wedi mynd rhagddo ers i bryderon gael eu codi rai blynyddoedd yn ôl. It provides physical health, mental health and well-being, while also providing opportunities to build community and bring people together. But barriers to participation can prevent people from accessing these benefits altogether. Sport Wales's 'State of the Nation' report for 2024-25 notes that two of the three factors most likely to encourage future participation in sport are if there were more facilities, clubs or groups in their area, and if it cost less.

There are pockets in my constituency of Caerdydd Ffynnon Taf, more specifically in Cardiff east, where public transport is infrequent and expensive. And with the decline in youth centres and community facilities in recent years following cuts, it feels as though this problem is only getting worse. I appreciate you've already answered part of this question, but I wanted to ask what action is being taken to measure and address transport-related barriers specifically, and how you're working with the Deputy Minister for Transport to make sure that there is participation for low-income families.

Any changes to the weighting of these indicators in the local government funding formula will have a huge impact on the ability of councils with the greatest population density and deprivation to deliver essential services. contributions.text_english: Diolch. On average, across Wales, around one in three children live in poverty, with some of the most deprived wards found in Clwyd, which is where I represent. We often talk about food poverty and fuel poverty, but I want to draw the Siambr's attention to another less visible consequence of poverty, and that is bed poverty. Too many children are sleeping in broken or unsuitable beds, having to share beds or regularly sleeping on sofas, chairs or even floors because they simply cannot afford an adequate bed. Sleep deprivation can affect almost every major system of the body. The introduction of the Cynnal payment is obviously very welcome, but we must ensure that this does not affect other means-tested benefits. Furthermore, if we're serious about creating lasting change for children living in poverty, we need the powers to tackle that poverty ourselves. I understand from news sources that there's been some discussion around this, but will the Minister commit to not only continuing discussions with the relevant departments to ensure Cynnal payments do not affect means-tested benefits, but also to pressing the UK Government for the full devolution of welfare powers to Wales?

Yesterday, the town of Porthmadog in my constituency marked the centenary of the death of one of its best-known sons, with a series of commemorative events. The name Eliseus Williams might not mean much to some, but I’m sure you will recognise his bardic name, Eifion Wyn.

Eifion Wyn was born at 28 New Street, Porthmadog, and although he spent time as a teacher at Snowdon Street school in the town, he is best known as one of the most popular poets of his time. He wrote in the wake of the Beirdd Newydd, a school of Welsh poets active in the final decades of the nineteenth century who emphasised that poetry should be lofty, serious, philosophical and profound.

Looking back, many consider the work of those poets to be obscure and abstruse. But Eifion Wyn was a poet of the people. It was important to him that his poetry was understandable and accessible, and that’s why he was such a popular poet. To quote an expert in the field, his poetry appealed to the people.

His legacy endures today, of course, not only in the name of the local primary school, but in his words. One of the most famous Welsh hymns, ‘Efengyl tangnefedd’, written by Eifion Wyn, is a call for international peace—a subject that is painfully relevant today. Thanks to the event organisers for all of their work.

Diolch. October is Black History Month. Remember the struggle, recognise the contribution and celebrate the achievement.

This Black History Month, we honour those who have helped build Wales, yet whose stories remain untold. I thank Race Council Cymru, Race Equality First, Ethnic Youth Support Team, Show Racism the Red Card, Black Lives Matter and Black History Cymru 365 campaigners, whose theme this year is 'Proud to be me'. I honour the Windrush generation too. I particularly recognise Professor Uzo Iwobi, founder of Race Council Cymru; Momena Ali, founder of EYST; and Shirley Au-Yeung of the Chinese in Wales Association. Their work in Swansea and beyond has opened doors for others.

To the black workers in the NHS, schools, public services, factories and the voluntary and third sectors, thank you. To the taxi drivers, takeaway owners, and corner shop keepers, thank you. Your contribution to our economy and communities is beyond measure. I am proud of the 'Anti-racist Wales Action Plan'. Its ambition must live in action and not simply words. I remember the late Mohammad Asghar, our first ethnic minority Assembly Member, elected for Plaid Cymru, and his service to this institution. And Betty Campbell, Wales's first black headteacher, who helped children dream beyond the barriers before them.

Black history is Welsh history. Black achievement is Welsh achievement. And with pride in our past, let us build change that will last. Diolch.

Diolch, Lywydd. I move the motion in the name of Lynne Neagle, and I am pleased to open today's debate on behalf of Welsh Labour.

Our intention for today's debate is to reach consensus on an issue that is so important to so many families across Wales. Whatever the political differences across this Chamber, we all want the best possible quality of life for children and adults with terminal illness. That's why Welsh Labour has tabled this motion: to champion the dedication and commitment of NHS and hospice workers who deliver dignity every day; to put on record our appreciation for the compassionate care they provide and the difference they make to people's lives; and to shine a light on the significant financial difficulties faced by hospices and the wider need for a sustainable solution to the funding of palliative and end-of-life care across Wales.

I'm pleased that other parties have chosen not to amend our motion today. The Senedd, passing this motion unanimously, would send a powerful message to our brilliant NHS staff and hospice workers, and it would challenge Ministers constructively to engage with this issue and to deliver on the commitment set out in the programme for government to address key challenges facing the sector.

Llywydd, last week I visited Tŷ Gobaith hospice just outside Conwy, and I heard first-hand about those challenges. Tŷ Gobaith provides high-quality, locally sensitive palliative and end-of-life care for children and young people. It's one of only two hospices providing specialist care for children in Wales, the other being Tŷ Hafan in Penarth. The staff at both do an incredible job. They help families create precious memories, they give children experiences and moments to cherish, and they allow parents the time and the space to enjoy being together as a family.

Behind those precious moments is specialist nursing and clinical care, support for children with complex life-limiting and life-threatening conditions and vital respite care for parents. Children's hospices support the whole family, often over many years, as well as providing care at the end of life and through bereavement. Right across Wales, dedicated hospice and NHS staff provide that personalised care every day. They manage people's pain, provide comfort and dignity, and support families through some of the most difficult times in their lives.

But alongside the exceptional care that I saw at Tŷ Gobaith, I also heard about the financial pressures they face, which I know are faced by hospices across Wales. Hospice UK and Hospices Cymru say that Wales's 15 charitable hospices care for over 20,000 children and adults affected by terminal illness. Hospice staff in Wales make around 77,000 visits to people in their own homes every year, helping people to remain in familiar surroundings and taking pressure off local hospitals. But the financial challenges are becoming increasingly difficult to manage across the sector.

Every hospice in Wales is forecasting a deficit budget for this financial year, forcing many to make difficult choices about their future, whether that's delaying recruitment, being unable to introduce new services, or even reducing services. On top of these pressures, Marie Curie estimate that the number of people in Wales needing palliative care will rise by 21 per cent by 2050, and their research also suggests that almost one in three adults in Wales have unmet palliative care needs, meaning around 10,000 people whose symptoms are not being managed and who lack the support they need. That's an increase of over 7,000 people needing care every year alongside significant unmet demand.

In Government, Welsh Labour recognised these concerns, increasing annual hospice funding and providing extra cost-of-living support to help protect vital services. We also delivered on our commitment to review hospice funding, which began with the development of new commissioning frameworks in partnership with the NHS and hospice sector. But as financial pressures intensify and demand still rises, there is a need for greater certainty and stability to protect services and help drive improvements. As Hospice UK and Hospices Cymru have argued, hospice funding needs to be stabilised in the short term and put on a sustainable footing in the long term. We need to consider how we can work towards meeting 30 per cent of agreed care costs in the hospice sector during this Senedd term.

In addition to a plan to stabilise the wider sector, there is a need to expand the offer for children and their families, with earlier access to support, better co-ordination between services and dependable respite and bereavement care wherever people live. And we need to ensure that our NHS and hospices have the workforce they need to meet growing demand, with the right staff in the right place.

We need to build on the Government's manifesto commitment to develop a new sustainable funding model, and to this end, Labour offers to work with the Government to address the key challenges facing palliative and end-of-life care as per the programme for government. That is what our motion is calling for. It's asking Ministers constructively to come forward with a long-term plan that stabilises and secures high-quality services and to ensure that our NHS and hospices have the skilled workforce they need to meet growing demand for palliative and end-of-life care.

These challenges require action now, as well as a clear plan for the future. Llywydd, we all recognise the extraordinary contribution that dedicated NHS and hospice staff make every day, delivering dignified and compassionate care to children and adults with terminal illness. We owe it to those staff and to the tens of thousands of families who depend on their care to ensure these services are protected for the future. It's vital that Ministers get this right and that we support Ministers in getting this right, and I hope Members will unanimously support this motion today. Diolch.

Hospices provide care and excellent support for children, young people and adults, and I want to share personal experience that demonstrates just how important this service is. Our daughter was born with cerebral palsy following complications during childbirth. She couldn't walk or use her hands, and for years, my wife and I were her main carers. During this challenging period, Tŷ Gobaith was a saviour for our family. It provided crucial respite, but far more than that too. The staff provided support, advice and professional care for us as a family.

One of the most difficult decisions for any parent is to accept that the life of their child may be short. Unfortunately, our daughter passed away at seven years of age. But the support of Tŷ Gobaith didn't stop at that point. The support continued through our bereavement, and counselling was available for our other daughters too. I will always be grateful for the care and compassion that was shown to our family by the staff at Tŷ Gobaith.

Llywydd, I'm pleased that we're having an opportunity to discuss an issue that is so important to so many families across Wales on the floor of this Chamber this afternoon. I'm also pleased to see that there is cross-party consensus in relation to the pressures facing hospices in Wales and the support required to meet their needs.

In the motion, the Labour Party is right to set out the significant financial pressures facing hospices in Wales, is right to call for a long-term plan to improve palliative care and end-of-life care, is right to make the case for a fair settlement for the sector in order to maintain a sustainable workforce. But with all due respect, Llywydd, it's important to note that it is Labour that has been in power for a quarter of a century and more. As a father and as a carer who has seen directly the challenges facing hospices, I do support this motion, but I have to admit my disappointment that more wasn't done by Labour during their time in power.

I welcome the motion and I'm pleased and proud that Plaid Cymru is now in charge and that we have a Government that is serious about addressing the complex and deep-seated challenges facing hospices, and I look forward to supporting this motion. Thank you.

The fundamental concept of our healthcare system in Wales is that it provides care free at the point of use from cradle to grave, and, unfortunately, it's the latter part of that statement that is at risk at the moment. It is the duty of our health services to ensure that people facing terminal illness and their families receive dignified and compassionate care at the end of life. Approximately 20,000 children and adults depend on our hospice services each year, and therefore they must be protected. But words alone won't protect them. Almost 30 per cent of Welsh voluntary hospices that were surveyed said that they had to reduce in-patient beds or services due to financial or workforce pressure already.

Several hospices across Wales have already closed, either permanently or temporarily, such as a four-bed unit in St David's Hospice in Holyhead. More than 70 per cent of hospices with in-patient units expect that cost pressures will make further beds unavailable. A significant majority of hospice care providers in Wales still depend on charitable donations. I'd like to thank the Welsh Labour Party for bringing forward this important debate this afternoon. My Welsh Conservative colleagues and I are pleased to be supporting this motion. Palliative and end-of-life care are incredibly important elements of our healthcare system, and we must do all that we can to ensure they are supported and protected for the future. It is not just about supporting people when they are coming towards the end of their lives. Palliative care is about supporting patients throughout, improving their quality of life and managing their pain. It is about treating people and their loved ones with dignity, compassion and respect at what is an incredibly emotional and difficult time. Our hospices play a vital role in delivering the care, whether that be onsite or, indeed, within people's homes, and I want to take a moment to thank the staff that are working in this sector. That includes the doctors, the nurses, the carers, the specialists, the volunteers, the hospice staff, the carers, and everyone else in between. They are the ones who are there day in, day out, supporting people through unimaginably upsetting times, bringing comfort, warmth and support. Their work is extraordinary, and it cannot, indeed, be an easy job.

I made a really sobering visit to St David's Hospice Care in Newport not too long ago, and I saw first-hand the compassion and dedication that the staff put into their roles. The services and support offered at the hospices were extensive, yet not a single penny is charged for the care that they provide. Despite that, it costs £15,000 every single day to provide that care, and while some funding is indeed provided from the Welsh Government and the NHS, it relies heavily on money raised through fundraising and charity shops. That should not be the case. Too many hospices are facing significant pressures and are in a similar boat when it comes to finance. Fundraising is often a great example of community spirit, bringing people together for a worthy cause, but it should not have to be relied on as much for such a service. It should complement public funding, not have to replace it. According to Hospice UK, around 70 per cent of the care costs of delivering hospice care are funded by charitable donations, while the remaining 30 per cent are provided by the Welsh Government and local health boards. That's staggering and, quite frankly, is not sustainable long term.

Around 20,000 adults and children every year are supported by Welsh hospices, and our ageing population makes the need for urgent improvements even more pressing. Presiding Officer, demand for hospice and palliative care continues to rise, but the cost pressures facing the sector are having a major impact. A survey carried out by Hospice UK revealed that more than 90 per cent of hospices in Wales are likely to cut certain services within the next 12 months to 24 months simply due to costs. Not only that, but near to one in two hospices already cut services last year, and I fear that if things do not improve, some hospices will be forced to close for good. We simply cannot allow that to happen.

A survey of 14 voluntary hospices in Wales discovered that 30 per cent are already reducing beds or cutting services, and that more than 70 per cent with in-patient units expect at least one bed to close either temporarily or permanently. Not only that, but three quarters fear that they will be forced to withdraw support normally provided by hospitals and care homes. These are, quite frankly, shocking statistics. But let me share an even more shocking and utterly distressing fact with you all: one in four people do not get the end-of-life care and support that they need, with someone dying without care and support every five minutes.

The Welsh Conservatives recognise the current pressures, and that's why we pledged to deliver a £40 million funding boost for the sector and ring-fenced support to meet half of the operating costs for children's hospices. But, crucially, we do believe that the Welsh Government should bring forward a sustainable funding model for hospices in Wales. It's clear that we need a new model, Presiding Officer, and I am pleased to see that the Welsh Government has committed to do that. So, I would welcome an update on this important piece of work when the Cabinet Minister responds to this debate.

However, we need action in the short term while the long-term funding model is indeed being drawn up to stabilise the sector, because hospices say that they need a one-off £5.5 million grant this financial year and an additional £8.2 million recurring funding from the draft budget of 2027-28. So, will the Cabinet Minister commit to this? I'd like to know what discussions he's had, on this finance, in relation to this, with his colleagues.

Rising costs are just one part of the challenge; workforce remains another significant barrier. In fact, some hospices are delaying recruitment and backfilling vacant positions due to the precarious financial position. The recruitment and retaining of specialist staff is indeed difficult—we all know it—and we need the Welsh Government to set out exactly what it's going to be doing to tackle this. But well-being is also a major concern. Caring for people approaching the end of life can indeed be emotionally demanding. High workload, staff sickness and limited resources can also contribute to stress, burnout and difficulties in retaining experienced staff. So, again, we need to hear from the Welsh Government how they're going to be addressing this challenge as well. Will this be a dedicated subsection in the Government's upcoming workforce plan?

As the motion sets out, we need to ensure that the Welsh NHS and hospices in Wales have the workforce that they need truly to deliver safe, high-quality and sustainable palliative care and end-of-life care. Whilst I'm talking about the motion, it would be remiss of me not to point out all of the things that could have been delivered by the Labour Party during their past 27 years stint here—and, sadly, they were not. In fact, when opposition parties challenged them to do so, the very things that they're calling for now, they made excuses as to why they could not do it.

So, as much as we do support today's motion, if the previous Welsh Labour Government had acted, we may not have needed to be here today debating this. But there's no point dwelling on the past; we need to look ahead and ensure the current Government takes robust action and protects hospice services.

I have visited Tŷ Olwen Hospice both as a relative and also as a Senedd representative of the area in which Tŷ Olwen is based. The issue that got me considering palliative care in detail, and hospices, was the assisted dying debate. The lack of adequate palliative care and end-of-life care and that it needs to be improved became immediately apparent. Palliative care offers physical, emotional and practical support to people with a terminal illness; it can be offered at any point after a terminal diagnosis. It was not only those suffering from motor neurone disease and other degenerative diseases who wished for the end-of-life option, but others with conditions who, with good palliative care, could have had a rewarding life.

First published in 2022, under a Labour Government, the palliative care quality statement set out high-level Welsh Government policy intentions for children's, young people's and adults' palliative and end-of-life care. The statement described what good-quality palliative and end-of-life care should look like. It listed six quality attributes: safe, timely, effective, person-centred, efficient, equitable.

Palliative care and end-of-life care is a critical part of our health and social care system. When it is got right, it can have a profound impact on people living with terminal illnesses and those close to them. Gaps in provision and a system under severe pressure mean that too many people are left without the care and support they need. Demand for palliative care and end-of-life care is growing. Marie Curie estimate that, by 2040, 37,000 people will need palliative and end-of-life care each year. With a system that cannot cope now, unless the Government treats this as a matter of urgency, there is very little chance of meeting future need. Clear leadership from the Welsh Government is needed to address the palliative and end-of-life care system.

I support Marie Curie's list of actions for the Government: ensure palliative and end-of-life care services are responsive to people's needs: high-quality care must be available in the right place at the right time in all parts of Wales; the Government must sustainably fund palliative and end-of-life services to meet the needs of all people living with a terminal illness across Wales; develop a palliative and end-of-life workforce that meets the growing need for care; ensure that all health and social care professionals have at least a foundation knowledge of palliative and end-of-life care; tell people living with terminal illnesses that a diagnosis could lead to death, tell them in language they can understand, and ensure people who are deaf, for example, have sign language interpreters available; patients need to be supported to have a conversation about their care preferences and have advance care plans in action; those who are terminally ill and those close to them, such as family, carers and friends, need 24-hour access to care, support and reassurance; ensure that people living with terminal illnesses are discharged from hospital swiftly when they are deemed able to return home; and appropriate support must be in place at the point of discharge, including support to die in their preferred place. This will, as well as benefiting terminally ill patients, free up beds in hospital and end the continual movement of those who are terminally ill into and out of hospital.

We cannot allow a postcode lottery for end-of-life care. Wherever you live in Wales, you need the same level of provision. With palliative care, there is a major role carried out by unpaid carers. The needs of unpaid carers have to be assessed and reviewed so that their needs can be met and the support they need can be provided. The difference that high-quality palliative care and end-of-life care can make for people living with a terminal illness, and those close to them, cannot be understated.

Too many in Wales cannot access the care they need. What we need is for health boards and trusts to periodically assess palliative and end-of-life care for their local population, then use that to inform service planning and delivery—these assessments to be made publicly available. Health boards must publish a local delivery plan for palliative care. These must set out how they will meet the population need and achieve the ambitions set out in the Welsh Government quality statement. All regional partnership boards must include palliative and end-of-life care leads to provide expert advice and guidance on meeting the needs of people with terminal illness and those close to them.

Can I just raise three matters from personal experience? A patient with cancer of the oesophagus who could not swallow was going to literally be left to starve to death until I intervened, and they had six months of a rewarding life by being PEG fed; a terminally ill patient without palliative care who just went in and out of hospital with no palliative-care support; a terminally ill patient left in a nursing home with no palliative support. All this needs funding. There is a need to establish a sustainable funding solution to establish a sustainable palliative care and end-of-life care system that can meet the growing need for care. There doesn't need to be a magic money tree—use unallocated resources, do what matters, instead of things such as a shadow broadcasting and communications authority for Wales. Palliative care and end-of-life care matter to me—do they matter to the Welsh Government?

Hospices provide the medical facilities needed to meet complex care needs, but they also provide comfort in a way hospitals just can't. A warm and personal welcome, a peaceful, homely feel, rather than cold, white, clinical walls, frightening noises, shared wards and the hustle and bustle of busy spaces.

A couple of weeks ago, I visited St Kentigern Hospice in St Asaph where I had an unexpected conversation with a resident named Mel. Mel was sitting outside enjoying his morning coffee. It was an ordinary, everyday moment, yet in many ways it represented everything that hospice care should be about: enabling people to enjoy the simple pleasures of life, retain their independence and experience moments of normality, even when facing the most difficult of circumstances. Mel spoke passionately about the compassion and care shown to him by the hospice staff and volunteers. He described how the people supporting him took time to understand his needs and tailor their care accordingly. This is what makes hospice care so special. It recognises that every patient is an individual with their own needs, wishes, fears and hopes. When a patient enters, they are defined by who they are and not what condition or illness they have. Every member of staff and every volunteer I encountered at St Kentigern's demonstrated a genuine commitment to providing comfort, compassion and dignity. It was clear that, to them, this wasn't a job, it was a vocation. Sadly, Mel passed away soon after our meeting, but I'm grateful to be able to say that his death was peaceful and dignified and that he was surrounded by love. The support provided by the hospice to Mel and his family played an important part in making that possible.

Between 2024 and 2025, hospices in Wales provided direct support to 4,900 family members, friends and carers. Caring for a loved one can be physically exhausting, emotionally draining and financially challenging. Unpaid carers give so much of themselves, often with little opportunity to rest and recover. Hospices can provide those carers with a much-needed break, helping them to recharge and continue in their caring role. Hospices also often continue to provide support long after a loved one has died. Bereavement services, counselling and practical guidance help families navigate the difficult journey that follows the loss of someone they love. So, when we talk of hospices and palliative care, we must look beyond the immediate care provided to patients. We must recognise the support given to families, unpaid carers, communities and the wider NHS. Hospices are precious institutions, but they cannot continue to deliver these services through goodwill and dedication alone. They need the resources, stability and support required to meet the growing needs of our communities. We must do all that we can to protect our hospices, support their dedicated staff and volunteers, and ensure that these services remain accessible to everybody, because everyone deserves the opportunity to live their final days with dignity, and no family should have to face the loss of a loved one without the care and support they need.

There is no second opportunity for a final conversation, no second opportunity to hold somebody's hand, no second opportunity to say what you wanted to say. Firstly, can I say 'thank you' to Welsh Labour for bringing forward this debate today? We've already heard how powerfully this issue affects people from across the Chamber. I've heard the passionate debate so far in this place and if you want to engage with that cross-party group, please look out for those all-important invites, but I know that we all have very busy diaries to contend with. But let me share with you, as Members, here today that we had a cross-party group meeting just this week and we announced that we're going to undertake an inquiry, as a cross-party group, into community-based palliative care and how that links into hospice care as well. I hope to have some recommendations that the cross-party group can bring to this Senedd as well. And I know that the Cabinet Minister will be interested to see how that may look and how that may shape some of his thinking in the months and years to come as well.

I want to echo the thanks and support already given to those working in this sector and recognise, as others have, the support that's given to around 20,000 children and adults in Wales every year, with that demand growing year in and year out. And we know of the pressure that that good work takes off the NHS, allowing patients to be discharged from hospital and offering 77,000 visits to people in their own homes annually as well.

We hear them desperate for certainty about what their future looks and feels like, and much of that does come down to funding. They need certainty over their budgets, over their funding; they need certainty over what services they can offer; they need certainty over whether Welsh Government will continue to enable them to provide care within our communities. Because if we cannot secure a sustainable funding plan for hospices for the duration of this Senedd term at least, we're at real risk of losing services or whole organisations in our communities, some of which we've already seen the evidence of.

I know the Cabinet Minister may point towards the national commissioning model that is being pulled together, perhaps, at the moment. My understanding is that that's likely to take between five and 10 years to come to fruition. I know the Cabinet Minister led an important debate in this place in January 2024, I believe it was, nearly three years ago, where, as a Chamber, we supported that position as well. But my concern, Cabinet Minister, is the timescale of this. It's nearly three years ago that you led that debate in this place. If that model takes another minimum of five years to develop, that's a long time of uncertainty for this sector. And the plea is that we create that certainty sooner rather than later.

They are of course grateful for those year-by-year allocations that are provided to them; they would not be able to survive without them. But what they do need is long-term, sustainable funding, and a long-term commissioning model to be delivered much sooner than the five to 10 years that perhaps is already being signalled. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

Shwmae, Lywydd; shwmae, bawb. Like my colleagues, I want to firstly start by thanking the staff, the volunteers, the carers, and the families who make palliative and end-of-life care possible across Wales. Now, as someone, like many of you, who would have cared for ageing parents, this debate is really important to me. I've been that family member who has had to sit down with a loved one and explain that there was nothing more that the NHS could do to cure their illness, and that the focus now had to be on keeping them comfortable, pain-free and supported at that time. 

And what our family learned very quickly was just how complex and overwhelming the palliative care system can be to navigate, and particularly when someone is living with multiple conditions and moving between hospital, community and home, and sometimes backwards and forwards. And, in our case, we were dealing with things like stroke, cancer, Parkinson's, motor neurone disease, and so much more, and repeated hospital admissions. And at every single stage, different professionals were then involved, different decisions had to be made, and new information had to be absorbed, and we were constantly paper chasing, trying to make sure we had the right letter and playing catch-up all the time. 

So, for families who are already coping with grief, uncertainty and exhaustion, navigating those systems can really be genuinely daunting. And that experience taught me that palliative care is much more than just medical treatment. It's about communication. It's about co-ordination. And it's also about ensuring that patients and families understand what support is actually available to them—who they can turn to, and what choices are genuinely open to them at that time of need. But most of all, this is about dignity. 

We all recognise the vital contribution that hospices make. They provide specialist care, emotional support, and, of course, practical help to patients and families across Wales. From my perspective, however, this has also got to be a workforce conversation as much as a funding conversation. Every hospice bed, every community visit, and every end-of-life care package depends on people—nurses, healthcare support workers, allied health professionals, social care workers, volunteers and, of course, unpaid carers. So, if we want sustainable palliative care, we need a sustainable workforce. And, as someone with roots in the trade union movement, I want to be clear about something else: caring has got to be valued. It must be valued. Those supporting patients and families at the end of their lives undertake some of the most emotionally demanding work in our society. They deserve secure employment; they deserve fair treatment, fair work, opportunities to develop their skills, and proper support, of course, for their own well-being at that time as well.

But sustainability, of course, is not enough on its own. We've also got to talk about equality and access. We know that not everyone experiences healthcare in the same way. People from black and Asian ethnic minority backgrounds can sometimes face barriers to accessing services. Disabled people may have additional communication, accessibility or support needs. LGBTQ+ people should have confidence that their identities and relationships will be respected. And Welsh language speakers should be able to receive care in the language that feels most natural and, of course, most comforting to them. 

And we must never of course forget unpaid carers who are balancing work, family responsibilities, and often their own health while caring for somebody else that they love. For me, therefore, the test of a successful palliative care system is not simply whether services exist; it's whether the person who needs that care can actually access it, understand it and receive it with dignity, regardless of their background, disability, language, postcode or personal circumstances.

And that brings me back to where I began. Behind every discussion about funding, workforce planning or service provision is a person approaching the end of their life, and a family who are just trying to support them through it. They shouldn't have to spend that precious time struggling to understand a complicated system or worrying about whether the help that they need will be there. Whatever our differences across this Chamber, I hope that we can agree on one fundamental principle: everyone in Wales deserves dignity, they deserve compassion, and they deserve respect at the end of life. All the people, of course, who provide that care, also deserve our support too. Diolch yn fawr.

Last night—or last week, rather—I was delighted to visit City Hospice in my constituency. They do fantastic work supporting people with terminal illnesses and their families. They provide care to people within their own homes, helping to keep them connected with their local communities and their support networks for as long as possible, but they also have an amazing drop-in centre in Whitchurch, with beautiful gardens and space for people to take part in meaningful activities, allowing people to keep on living well right to the end of their lives.

They told me about a man they supported who was understandably feeling very low and said that one of the things he was really missing was the opportunity to chat about football, so they created a sports bar where people could drink alcohol-free beer, watch football matches and talk about them, often with a sporting hero as a special guest. I confess that's not something that appeals to me at all personally, but the sports bar has now become one of their most popular activities. This is the real difference that hospices make in people's lives, but this vital work is at risk without sustainable funding and strong collaborative working with local health boards.

The previous Government took steps towards developing a hospice commissioning framework to ensure consistent good practice across Wales. However, I understand there are still significant variations across different areas. The Welsh hospice sector needs an additional £5.5 million of funding this year and an additional £8.2 million of funding in each subsequent year of the Senedd term. This works out at around, as people have said, £30 million for the whole of this Senedd term, which is not a great deal amount of money considering the hugely beneficial impacts for our communities.

On average, Welsh hospices get only around a third of their income from statutory sources and must fundraise for the rest from private donors, which is extremely difficult in the context of the cost-of-living crisis. Any additional financial help for hospices would of course be welcomed, but long-term certainty in both the contracts and grant funding, so that staff and service users can be confident their vital services will be there whenever they are needed. Predictable, multi-year recurring funding allows hospices to better plan ahead and supports their highly skilled staff with a huge number of different medical specialisms embedded within their own local communities.

I'm glad that we all agree that the incredible work of our hospices and palliative care workers is not just worth celebrating in this debate this afternoon, but also worthy of fair and sustainable funding in recognition of their life-affirming work. Diolch.

Diolch, Llywydd, and I'd like to thank everyone for sharing their personal stories today. How we care for people in the final chapters of their lives is the ultimate measure of our compassion, our values and our society. Palliative and end-of-life care is not a secondary branch of medicine; it is a fundamental pillar in a truly integrated health and social care system.

In Neath Port Talbot, Marie Curie estimates that 1,550 people would have benefited from palliative and end-of-life care in 2023. In 10 years, they estimate that demand for palliative care in Neath Port Talbot will increase to 1,705 people per year, and what we must remember is that behind every figure, there is a person, there is a family.

Early identification of needs through health boards is vital to inform the planning and delivery of services. I was pleased to see in the Plaid Cymru manifesto commitments to ensure that every regional partnership board includes a palliative and end-of-life care need, because dignity in death should never depend on your postcode.

And we turn to the staff of our hospices across Wales. The support these individuals provide to families could never be measured—the care, experience and compassion enabling people to stay in their homes and communities wherever possible. But an ageing population with increasingly complex conditions means that pressures on our front-line staff will only intensify. If we do not build a resilient community care network, our emergency services will bear the brunt. People who wish to spend their final days in the comfort of their own homes surrounded by their loved ones will continue to be trapped in hospital beds because the community support simply isn't there. I'm glad to see the consensus across the Chamber today to work together to ensure that every individual in Wales can face the end of their life with dignity, comfort and peace.

I would like to see that you've listened and are going to act now you're in Government to deliver for this key sector, and deliver for those families and people across Wales who are relying on you to stand up to your promises. Thank you.

Thank you very much, Llywydd, and I welcome the opportunity to respond to this important debate. I'm also grateful to Ken Skates for bringing it before the Senedd today. I'd also like to thank all Members for their poignant contributions during this debate. This is an issue on which there is a great deal of common ground across the Chamber. There is much in today's motion that we could all agree with.

High-quality palliative and end-of-life care is exceptionally important. It means that people are treated with dignity, compassion and care. That's important to the individual. It's important to families and to carers as well, and it is just as important to the people who support them through some of the most difficult times that they will ever face. Hospices are a crucial part of that care. They provide valuable clinical expertise. They help people to live as well as they can. They work hand in hand with the NHS and community services to provide care that is compassionate and focused on the individual.

I have visited a number of hospices myself, first as an opposition politician, and now as a Minister in Government, and on every occasion, I've been struck by the dedication of the staff, the volunteers and everyone else who is part of their work. I'm sure that I speak on behalf of the whole Chamber when I say that we owe a great debt of gratitude to them.

I fully understand the concerns that have been raised today regarding the pressures that face the sector, and I sympathise entirely with them. Indeed, many of the matters that have been highlighted today were matters that I myself raised when I was on the opposition benches, as we have heard. They were important then, and they remain important today. The financial situation is challenging, and I will not pretend otherwise. Hospices have been clear about the pressures that face the sector: higher energy costs, increases in national insurance contributions, increased demand for services, and uncertainty regarding commissioning arrangements.

I heard those concerns directly when I met with Hospices Cymru recently. We discussed the pressures currently facing the sector. We also discussed the longer term and what needs to be done to place hospice services on a more sustainable footing.

However, recognising the constraints doesn't mean accepting that nothing can be done. There are practical steps that we can and must take to improve services and strengthen planning. Our programme for government contains a clear commitment to address the key challenges facing palliative and end-of-life care. My officials are already working with colleagues across health, social care, regional partnerships and the unpaid carers agenda, to turn that commitment into practical action.

The national service specification supports more consistent planning and delivery. The national competency framework supports workforce development, while the hospice commissioning approach establishes principles for more consistent and sustainable arrangements. The workforce point in the motion is particularly important. The national competency framework provides an important foundation for ensuring staff across health and care have the skills and confidence needed to deliver high-quality palliative and end-of-life care. Palliative care must also be recognised earlier and embedded across the pathways through which people receive care. Through the development of our national cancer strategy and acute and emergency care framework, we are looking at how specialist palliative support can be better integrated across services, supporting earlier access to care, stronger advanced care planning, and more joined-up support for patients and families.

Llywydd, I also want to address the call for fair and sustainable hospice funding. Current arrangements have developed differently across Wales. Hospices have told us that inconsistency and uncertainty make it more difficult to plan services, retain their workforce and invest for the future. Too often, access to palliative and end-of-life care can still be influenced by where people live or how services have developed historically. That variation is not in the interests of patients, families or the wider system. The hospice commissioning guidance gives us a common direction, but its publication was not the end of the process.

The next phase must be about implementation. This includes a national population needs assessment, and work on future commissioning and funding models. The national palliative and end-of-life care programme is working to build a clearer understanding of need across Wales, so that decisions reflect what people require rather than simply reflecting historical patterns of provision. We want to make meaningful progress towards more consistent and sustainable arrangements during this Senedd term. I recognise the sector wants greater certainty and I share that goal. Our focus now is on implementing the commissioning approach and ensuring funding decisions are informed by evidence, agreed service expectations and clearer accountability.

But our attention isn't limited to the longer term. We will continue to pursue practical opportunities to support hospices with immediate pressures, while continuing this wider reform programme. A recent example is the agreement of £800,000 through the all-Wales capital programme to support the redevelopment of City Hospice. Whilst investment in one project can't resolve the pressures facing the sector as a whole, it demonstrates that we are supporting services now while developing more sustainable arrangements for the future. It's also vital that we set a clear, shared policy direction bringing together services, workforce, commissioning, funding, and support for families and carers.

And we're not starting from a blank page, although we recognise there is always room to improve. The quality statement for palliative and end-of-life care, which sets the strategic expectations across health, social care and the third sector, is currently being refreshed and, alongside the existing suite of supporting documents, will help provide the strategic framework for the next phase of improvement.

However, ultimately, national frameworks must become practical action on the ground. Through my recent discussions with the sector, including at an event hosted by Marie Curie and Hospice UK, I have heard a very clear message. There is a genuine appetite for collaboration and an appetite to improve the care and support available to people as they approach the end of their lives. That's why I have asked officials to start the work of preparing for a national summit on palliative and end-of-life care. We intend to hold it next March.

I want that summit to bring together the NHS, hospices and other stakeholders. I want it to help to shape future priorities for palliative and end-of-life care in Wales. The intention is not to commission another report, nor to rehearse the challenges that we already understand. The intention is to bring people together around a clear programme of action and delivery during this Senedd term.

Llywydd, I do not underestimate the scale of the challenges that face the sector. I also understand full well the concerns stemming from uncertainty on funding and the workforce. But, at the same time, it is important to recognise the progress that has already been made. It is also important that we maximise the opportunities ahead of us.

Behind every discussion on funding, commissioning and the workforce are real people and real families—people who face some of the most difficult circumstances that any one of us could imagine. They deserve compassionate care, fair care, and care that is available when it is needed most. We have an opportunity during this Senedd term to make a genuine difference by working together across the NHS, hospices, local government and the third sector. By doing that, we can create a more sustainable and more consistent system—a system that puts people at the heart of the care provided.

That is the task that we have committed to as a Government, and that's the task that we will be taking forward in partnership with everyone who plays such an important part in providing palliative and end-of-life care the length and breadth of Wales. Thank you, Llywydd.

Diolch, Lywydd. Today we do have a cosy consensus. It's one that crosses all parties, and it concerns such a vital area of care that's needed at the end of life and when facing terminal illness. There have been many incredibly valuable contributions, which I have, I'm afraid, too little time available to do justice to. We began with Elfed Williams, who shared his very personal experience of the care provided by hospices and their remarkable staff. He reflected, I think, what many subsequently talked about: just how important it is to give our thanks to the people who make end-of-life experiences and terminal illness manageable.

Benjamin Hodge Mckenna reiterated the pressures facing hospices, outlining the future needs of people with palliative and end-of-life care requirements. Natasha Asghar so rightly identified the compassion and the dignity needed by and provided to children and adults in need of palliative and end-of-life care. St David's hospice in Newport is indeed a remarkable place, and Natasha highlighted workforce issues, including staff well-being. Mike Hedges has long championed the work of hospices and NHS staff, who care for people with terminal illness, and he outlined why high-quality care must be available to people in all parts of Wales. Tŷ Gobaith covers a vast area, and I was told on my visit about the particular challenges of people in remote and rural areas. Mike, along with Rebeca Phillips, rightly called for care not to be subject to a postcode lottery and to ensure equal access for all.

Becca Martin shared what she was told by Mel and presented what I thought was a powerful case, with real emotional depth, for greater support for carers to receive vital respite care. Bereavement support, as Becca outlined, continues through and beyond bereavement, often for many months, potentially even years. Cristiana Emsley also shared a deeply personal experience, reminding us of the need and unmet need across our society. This time last year, Marie Curie nurses provided exceptional end-of-life care for my mum, and she was able to come home to die in dignity and familiar surroundings. I think all of us will know of, or eventually need ourselves, the care of angels at the end of our lives.

Sam Rowlands rightly praised Mark Isherwood for his work in this area, and also Jayne Bryant for her work. And Sam, as chair of the all-party group, I'm sure there's nothing that I can say about this subject that you don't already know, but you were absolutely right to say that certainty of funding is the central ask of hospices. And today I think we heard cross-party support for this to be delivered.

Shav Taj identified how important communication is in finding appropriate care, and Shav was absolutely right to call for fair work, respect, care and support for the workforce. Paul Rock gave us an insight into the operation of hospice sports bars and the way that innovation and person-centred care can enhance palliative and end-of-life experiences. And James Evans shared with us his experience of visiting the phenomenal hospice Tŷ Hafan. He also reiterated the need for funding certainty and fairness of access.

Minister, I believe you gave us assurance, the assurance that we were looking for in this motion, that work will continue and intensify in an area of care so important across political lines and across the communities that we all serve. I'm sure that Members right across this Chamber are keen to help in that work and will scrutinise its progress.

Now, in Government, we increased annual hospice funding and provided extra cost-of-living support to help protect vital services. But unmet and increasing need requires a concerted effort backed by all parties. I fear there will be very few and precious opportunities like this in the coming three and a half years to have consensus and to rally behind an area of delivery that is so important to all. But it is essential that we act collectively and respectfully on such important matters. Care in death is just as important as care at birth. I thank the Minister and all Members who have contributed to this debate, and I hope that we will achieve complete consensus at the vote.

Environmental stewardship should not belong to one political party, one ideology, or one side of the Chamber. It should be a common cause. For small c conservatives, environmental conservation is central to our political philosophy. Yes, too often the tradition is overlooked because the debate about the environment has become almost entirely dominated by carbon reduction, which, whilst important, should not dominate Government action over other concerns. Many to the right, myself included, object to the direction of current environmental policy, but we should not allow that disagreement to be mistaken for indifference towards the environment itself. I believe climate change is a serious, potentially existential challenge that must be addressed, and we cannot simply ignore the evidence to pretend that a changing climate presents no risks, but we must distinguish between the challenge we face and the policies Governments choose to pursue in response to it.

I have profound concerns about the approach to net zero. The UK can impose ever more ambitious targets on itself and introduce costly regulations, but climate change is a global problem driven by global emissions. The effectiveness of our response must therefore be judged in a global context. My concern is that policies pursued in the name of net zero will make little difference to the global climate trajectory if they are not matched by meaningful international action, while not imposing enormous costs on ordinary people here at home, because those costs are not borne equally. We should not ask people on the lowest incomes to shoulder disproportionate costs for policies whose global impact depends on what the rest of the world does, when the UK's impact is so minuscule.

If the United Kingdom reached net zero by next week, would the climate stop changing? Of course it would not. That does not mean we should abandon efforts to reduce emissions, it means we should pursue them sensibly, in concert with other countries, and in a way that is economically sustainable and commands public support.

We should also be honest about the need to adapt to the changes in climate we face. We need resilient infrastructure, effective flood prevention, healthy soils, restored peatlands, and landscapes better equipped to withstand drought, wildfire and extreme rainfall. We must also consider the standardisation of air conditioning in homes and schools, and fund agricultural science that looks at how crops may have to adapt to a changing climate.

Mitigation and adaptation must go hand in hand, but my concern is that the single-minded focus of carbon targets has distracted us from other pressing environmental problems—problems where we could make tangible difference to people's lives and the natural world around us.

As we have been racing towards ever more ambitious carbon targets, our rivers and our seas have been filling with sewage. Natural Resources Wales reported that Dŵr Cymru was responsible for 155 pollution incidents in 2024. That was the highest number of sewage pollution incidents recorded by the company in a decade. We should be just as determined to stop sewage entering our rivers as we are to meet carbon targets.

Another area where we should be able to find common ground is the protection of our habitats and our beautiful landscapes. Species are disappearing, habitats are under pressure and too many landscapes are failing to reach their ecological potential. Tree planting, habitat restoration, healthier soils and protecting native species can all make a real difference, but this must be done in partnership with farmers and landowners, not through top-down diktats. We should reward long-term stewardship rather than simply measuring compliance with administrative requirements. We also need tougher penalties for environmental crime and better policing. While law-abiding citizens face increasingly costly waste disposal, criminals are dumping toxic waste and despoiling our countryside with apparent impunity.

Michael Sheen's recent documentary Buried has highlighted the illegal dumping of forever chemicals and acid sludge across England and Wales. In March, Natural Resources Wales reported that nearly 50,000 fly-tipping incidents had been recorded in Welsh local authorities in the previous year—an increase of almost 15 per cent. That's about 133 incidents every day. We need effective investigations and meaningful penalties. This is not about punishing well-meaning landowners for missing a clause in a regulation; it's about ensuring that those who wantonly destroy our natural environment face prison.

Presiding Officer, this brings me back to the central argument of this debate: environmental policy should not be judged solely on carbon targets, but by whether our rivers are cleaner, our habitats are recovering, our wildlife is thriving and our countryside is protected for future generations. Achieving this means working with farmers, landowners, conservationists, volunteers, communities and businesses. Good environmental policy need not be prohibitively expensive. Often, the best solutions are practical, locally led and rooted in an understanding of the landscapes. We can disagree about net zero and the pace of decarbonisation, but surely we can agree that sewage should not pollute our rivers, that endangered species should be protected, illegal dumping should be punished and those restoring habitats should be encouraged rather than obstructed. These aren't left-wing or right-wing objectives; they're commonsense objectives.

I'm confident the new Minister for climate change and rural resilience shares my desire to put sound land management and the protection of our natural inheritance at the heart of environmental policy, and I look forward to hearing how he intends to deliver that. Our responsibility as custodians is to ensure the next generation inherits a natural environment richer, healthier and better protected than the one we inherited. That's what environmental stewardship means to me. I look forward to hearing the other contributors to the debate. Thank you.

We're told that even though Britain only emits 1 per cent of global carbon dioxide emissions, whilst China and India emit 40 per cent, we should pursue net zero as an example. Ironically, our main emissions cuts have come from exporting steel and other heavy industries to those same countries. But they cannot follow our example; they cannot export their emissions to themselves, and the goods we now import are often produced under weaker environmental rules.

Net zero in its current form is ideologically driven, it is damaging our economy and it will not deliver its aims. We need to look after the environment without crippling our industry or sacrificing our energy security. Nuclear power offers that practical path. It's carbon neutral, highly reliable and statistically the safest form of large-scale energy. Yes, the upfront costs and build times are significant, but the long-term benefits outweigh them. It's time to stop delaying. Let's re-industrialise, invest in nuclear and protect both our economic and environmental future. Thank you.

I'd like to thank David Mills for bringing forward this debate and giving me a slot to speak.

Environmental stewardship should be common ground across this Chamber, not because the challenges are easy, but because they affect every community in Wales. As a member of the climate change committee, I'm acutely aware of the scale of those challenges. Nearly one in five assessed species in Wales is now threatened with extinction, and species abundance has fallen by around 20 per cent in a generation. In Ceredigion Penfro, those pressures are felt in the rivers, peatlands and coastal habitats that define our communities. We're fortunate to be home to the Dyfi UNESCO biosphere, Cardigan Bay and some of Wales's most important marine and terrestrial wildlife habitats. They're not only environmental assets, they're economic assets too.

This debate should not simply be about what we stand to lose; it should be about what we stand to gain. The transition to a low-carbon economy presents major opportunities for Wales—opportunities to create jobs, attract investment, strengthen energy security and support thriving rural economies. The same is true for nature recovery. Whether it is tackling agricultural pollution, restoring peatlands, improving river quality or supporting sustainable food production, there are solutions that can work for nature and for people. We need to move beyond denial, beyond blame and beyond the sense of hopelessness that too often creeps into these discussions. Instead, we need leadership, we need collaboration—and I agree that should extend to international collaboration—and we need the confidence to seize the opportunities that come from responding to the climate and nature emergencies together. Because, if Wales gets this right, environmental stewardship will not just protect what we value, it will help build a more resilient, prosperous and sustainable future for all our communities. Diolch.

We're developing, as Members know, Wales's first climate and nature action plan. It'll bring together actions across government and across society to restore nature, to strengthen climate resilience, to support sustainable development, setting out a pathway towards our ambition in relation to net zero, but also substantive nature recovery as well. And a just transition will be baked into our approach, so that we avoid some of the mistakes that have happened in the past where some communities have been damaged and left behind by much of this.

But, of course, it isn't a binary policy, because retrofitting homes provides people with support for the cost-of-living crisis because it will lower bills. More energy-efficient homes will mean lower energy bills. Retrofitting homes means jobs. People will need to be employed to retrofit those homes, bringing further economic benefits. It'll give people warmer homes to live in. And that, in itself, I think is something that we should aspire to. But there are health benefits from that as well, because we will see, as a consequence of people not living in cold and damp homes, fewer children being raised in those homes and consequently suffering from respiratory challenges. We will see fewer winter excess deaths amongst our older population. So, net zero isn't binary. It's an opportunity to bring a number of additional benefits with it.

It's practical delivery for climate and nature together.

But restoration can't be limited to individual habitats or protected sites. Nature recovery is needed across productive farmland, yes, but in our towns and communities as well. And, of course, Government can't deliver all of this alone. Through Nature Networks, we've announced more than £10 million for the next funding round. The fund has already supported more than 125 projects, improving protected sites and ecological connections across Wales.

Motion NDM9329 Lynne Neagle

To propose that the Senedd:

1. Appreciates and values the palliative and end-of-life care provided across the Welsh NHS and hospices.

2. Recognises the vital role played by hospices in Wales in providing specialist palliative and end-of-life care.

3. Notes the significant financial pressures facing hospices in Wales and the call from Hospice UK and Hospices Cymru for additional funding to protect hospice services.

4. Calls on the Welsh Government to:

a) develop a long-term plan to improve palliative and end-of-life care across Wales, ensuring high-quality services are available to everyone who needs them;

b) set out how it will deliver fair and sustainable funding for hospices across Wales; and

c) ensure that the Welsh NHS and hospices in Wales have the workforce they need to deliver safe, high-quality and sustainable palliative and end-of-life care.

Cynnig NDM9329 Lynne Neagle

Cynnig bod y Senedd:

1. Yn gwerthfawrogi ac yn gweld gwerth yn y gofal lliniarol a diwedd oes a ddarperir ar draws GIG a hosbisau Cymru.

2. Yn cydnabod y rôl hanfodol a chwaraeir gan hosbisau yng Nghymru wrth ddarparu gofal lliniarol arbenigol a gofal diwedd oes.

3. Yn nodi'r pwysau ariannol sylweddol sy'n wynebu hosbisau yng Nghymru a'r alwad gan Hospice UK a Hospices Cymru am gyllid ychwanegol i ddiogelu gwasanaethau hosbisau.

4. Yn galw ar Lywodraeth Cymru i:

a) datblygu cynllun hirdymor i wella gofal lliniarol a gofal diwedd oes ledled Cymru, gan sicrhau bod gwasanaethau o ansawdd uchel ar gael i bawb sydd eu hangen;

b) nodi sut y bydd yn darparu cyllid teg a chynaliadwy ar gyfer hosbisau ledled Cymru; ac

c) sicrhau bod gan GIG Cymru a hosbisau yng Nghymru y gweithlu sydd ei angen arnynt i ddarparu gofal lliniarol a gofal diwedd oes diogel, o ansawdd uchel a chynaliadwy.
